demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette: She stands at her drafting table, pencil hovering over a scaled detail of a residential balcony. At forty-seven, her hands no longer tremble when they draw, but they freeze at the sight of structural annotations. Three years ago, she misses a decimal point in the rebar spacing. The scaffolding collapses during a summer inspection. A junior draftsman falls fourteen feet. He walks now with a cane, but he never returns to the firm. In the months that follow, she stops entering construction sites. She tells her colleagues it is a matter of accessibility, but the truth lives in her chest: she cannot stand the smell of wet concrete, the whine of overhead cranes, or the particular silence that falls when everyone stops working. She begins leaving early, claiming client deadlines. She starts taking the long way home, routing her car past three extra intersections just to avoid the hospital where he is treated. Sleep fractures. She wakes at 2:14 a.m. every night, heart hammering, convinced she hears the sound of metal shearing. Her work changes. Where she once designs with fluid confidence, she now measures twice, then measures again. She prints every specification, highlights them in yellow, and emails them to three different reviewers. Her husband, David, watches her trace the same beam cross-section for an hour, his fingers drumming a quiet rhythm on the kitchen counter. He learns not to ask what she is working on. He knows that if he touches her drafting ruler, she flinches. The memories do not arrive as stories. They arrive as sensations. The weight of a clipboard against her palm. The smell of rust and rain. The exact pitch of a voice calling her name before the fall. She hears it in the hum of her refrigerator. She feels it in the sudden drop of an elevator. When she catches her reflection in a shop window, she stops walking, waiting for the ground to tilt. David holds her through these moments, but she starts sleeping in the guest room. She tells herself it is for his back. She knows it is because she does not want him to see her jump when the house settles. Her grandmother’s proverbs still guide her. In her West African family, resilience is taught as quiet endurance. Amara tries to honor that. She attends the same church she has sat in since childhood, nodding through sermons about grace, her lips moving along the words while her hands remain clenched in her lap. She volunteers at a children’s literacy program, but she only reads the books with thick, padded covers. She cannot bear the sound of pages turning too fast. In her third session, she arrives with a portfolio. She places it on my desk without opening it. “I’m designing a new library,” she says, her voice steady. “It will have no sharp corners. All load-bearing walls will be double-stud. The floor plan will be reviewed by four independent engineers.” She pauses, then adds, “I still check the calculations myself.” She does not look at me. She looks at the window, at the street below, at anything that does not require her to sit in the space between us. I notice how she sits on the edge of the chair, knees together, shoulders drawn forward, as if bracing for an impact that has already passed. The room is quiet. The pencil on her desk remains still.
